prompt: In the `relctl` CLI, why does each subcommand (`tag`, `promote`, `status`) create its own `flag.NewFlagSet` instead of parsing all flags from one global flag set?
choices: So each subcommand can define and parse its own flags (like --version) independently, without colliding with another subcommand's flags of the same name
Because Go's flag package cannot parse boolean flags from a global flag set
Because os.Args can only be read once per process, so each subcommand needs a fresh copy
So each subcommand can run in its own separate OS process

prompt: In `relctl`, exit code 64 is used when the subcommand name is missing or unrecognized, following the BSD sysexits.h convention. What does that exit code represent?
choices: A usage error (EX_USAGE) — the invocation itself was wrong, not a runtime failure
Successful completion with no changes made
A transient failure that the caller should retry automatically
The process was terminated by an external signal

prompt: In the hand-written client-go controller, what does calling `queue.AddRateLimited(key)` after a failed `syncHandler` call do differently from calling `queue.Add(key)`?
choices: It requeues the key after an exponentially increasing delay based on how many times that key has already failed, instead of requeuing it immediately
It permanently removes the key from the queue so it is never retried
It immediately retries the key on a different goroutine in parallel
It pauses the entire informer's watch until the key succeeds

prompt: The lesson rebuilds Tier 4's RedisCluster reconcile loop directly against client-go instead of controller-runtime. What does this expose that controller-runtime's Reconciler interface normally hides?
choices: The SharedIndexInformer and workqueue plumbing that turns raw watch events into deduplicated, retried, backed-off sync calls
The OpenAPI schema validation that the API server performs on CRD objects
The etcd storage format used to persist custom resources
The kubelet's container runtime interface for starting pods

prompt: Why does `subresources: status: {}` on the RedisCluster CRD (from Tier 4) matter for the reconcile loop built in this lesson?
choices: It splits /status onto its own API endpoint, so the operator's status writes don't bump the same generation/update event that would re-enqueue and re-trigger the reconciler forever
It tells the API server to validate the status field against a stricter OpenAPI schema than the spec field
It makes status updates faster by skipping etcd persistence entirely
It is required before kubectl can display the object's status column at all

prompt: A CI pipeline runs `prune && deploy`, trusting prune's exit code to decide whether to proceed. Which design choice most directly protects that pipeline across upgrades to prune's own version?
choices: Keeping exit code meanings stable release to release (never silently repurposing what 0, 1, or 2 mean)
Printing a colorful progress bar while artifacts are being deleted
Renaming flags each release to reflect the current implementation details
Always exiting 0 regardless of outcome so the pipeline never blocks

prompt: A Terraform provider's Read function, called during `terraform plan`, is best understood as playing which role relative to a Kubernetes operator's Reconcile function?
choices: The same desired-vs-observed state comparison as Reconcile, but pull-triggered on demand by `plan` rather than push-triggered by a persistent watch
A completely unrelated mechanism, since Terraform has no notion of observed state at all
A function that only runs once, at provider installation, and never again
A replacement for Create and Update that makes them unnecessary

prompt: In the badly-designed `prune` tool shown in the lesson, which detail is the clearest sign of an API that is unsafe to depend on in automation?
choices: It exits 0 even when some deletions failed partway through, so a pipeline gating on `$?` can't detect the partial failure
It accepts a --dry-run flag before deleting anything
It prints a human-readable summary line at the end of a successful run
It uses Go's flag package instead of a third-party argument-parsing library
